title: Neighbours Trading Places
statement: Find the number of six-digit positive integers $N$, with non-zero leading digit, that have the following property: for each of the five pairs of adjacent digit positions of $N$, interchanging the two digits in those positions and leaving the other four digits unchanged gives a number divisible by $7$. If an interchange places a $0$ in the leading position, the result is read as an ordinary integer with that leading zero ignored.
hints: Write $N = \sum_{i=0}^{5} d_i \cdot 10^i$ and find how much the value of $N$ changes when the digits at place values $10^i$ and $10^{i+1}$ are interchanged. Look at the differences $e_i = d_i - d_{i+1}$.

Work in modular arithmetic modulo $7$. An interchange changes $N$ by $9 \cdot 10^i \cdot e_i$, where $e_i = d_i - d_{i+1}$, so each condition fixes $e_i$ as a multiple of $N$ modulo $7$. Note that the statement does not say $7 \mid N$. To find $N$ modulo $7$, rewrite $N$ using $d_5$ and the $e_i$; the coefficients are repunits, and $7 \mid 111111$.

Substituting the values of $e_i$ into that expression for $N$ gives $N \equiv 6N \pmod 7$, so $7 \mid N$ and every $e_i$ is divisible by $7$. Hence the six digits all lie in one residue class modulo $7$, and any such number has the property. It remains to count these numbers class by class, taking care with the class $\{0, 7\}$, where the leading digit cannot be $0$.
solution: Write $N = \sum_{i=0}^{5} d_i \cdot 10^i$ and let $e_i = d_i - d_{i+1}$ for $0 \le i \le 4$. Interchanging the digits at place values $10^i$ and $10^{i+1}$ gives the integer $N + 9 \cdot 10^i \cdot e_i$, and this formula still holds if a $0$ reaches the leading position, since that $0$ contributes nothing to the value. Modulo $7$ we have $9 \equiv 2$ and $10 \equiv 3$, so the five conditions are $2 \cdot 3^i \cdot e_i \equiv -N \pmod 7$. Multiplying by $3 \cdot 5^i$ and using $6 \equiv -1$ and $15 \equiv 1$ gives $e_i \equiv 3 \cdot 5^i \cdot N \pmod 7$. Therefore $e_0 \equiv 3N$, $e_1 \equiv N$, $e_2 \equiv 5N$, $e_3 \equiv 4N$ and $e_4 \equiv 6N$. Since $d_i = d_5 + e_i + e_{i+1} + \dots + e_4$, collecting the coefficient of each $e_j$ in $N$ gives $1 + 10 + \dots + 10^j$, so $$N = 111111 \cdot d_5 + e_0 + 11 \cdot e_1 + 111 \cdot e_2 + 1111 \cdot e_3 + 11111 \cdot e_4.$$ Now $111111 = 7 \cdot 15873$, and $11$, $111$, $1111$, $11111$ are congruent to $4$, $6$, $5$, $2$ modulo $7$. Substituting the values of $e_i$ gives $$N \equiv (3 + 4 + 30 + 20 + 12) \cdot N = 69 \cdot N \equiv 6N \pmod 7.$$ Thus $5N \equiv 0 \pmod 7$, so $7 \mid N$. Then every $e_i \equiv 0 \pmod 7$, which means all six digits are congruent modulo $7$. Conversely, suppose all six digits of $N$ are congruent to $r$ modulo $7$. After any interchange, every digit is still congruent to $r$, so the resulting number is congruent to $r \cdot (1 + 10 + \dots + 10^5) = r \cdot 111111 \equiv 0 \pmod 7$. So the property holds exactly when all six digits lie in one residue class modulo $7$. The digit classes modulo $7$ are $\{0, 7\}$, $\{1, 8\}$, $\{2, 9\}$, $\{3\}$, $\{4\}$, $\{5\}$ and $\{6\}$. In the class $\{0, 7\}$ the leading digit must be $7$ and the other five digits are free, giving $2^5 = 32$ numbers. The classes $\{1, 8\}$ and $\{2, 9\}$ give $2^6 = 64$ numbers each, and the four singleton classes give $1$ number each. The total is $32 + 2 \cdot 64 + 4 = 164$. The answer is $164$. Why this works. modular-arithmetic, place-value-representation: writing $N$ through its adjacent digit differences turns the five interchange conditions into a single congruence $N \equiv 6N$ modulo $7$, which forces all the differences to vanish.
